summary: This standards-track RFC defines how the Opus interactive speech and audio codec is encapsulated in Ogg, so Opus-encoded data can be stored in an Ogg logical bitstream.

eli5.summary: Opus is a way to squeeze sound into small data. This says how to pack that into an Ogg file.

questions: how is opus stored in ogg files
what is the opus file extension
what is the opus channel mapping family
subtitle: How Opus audio is packed into Ogg files and streams: headers, timing, channel layouts and metadata.

tldr.problem: The Opus codec produces packets of compressed audio, but it needs a container that provides metadata, seeking, corruption detection, recovery after errors and the ability to share a stream with other media.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7845 puts Opus packets into the Ogg container: an ID header page first, then a comment header, then audio pages whose granule positions count 48 kHz samples. A pre-skip value and a channel mapping handle codec delay and surround layouts.
tldr.outcome: The same format works for files on disk and for live streams. The RFC also registers the .opus extension and an IANA registry of channel mapping families. It is updated by RFC 8486.

facts.label: Packet duration
facts.value: Multiples of 2.5 ms, up to 120 ms

today: RFC 7845 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5334 and is itself updated by RFC 8486. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Opus in an Ogg Container
sections.content:
The Opus codec is a low-latency audio codec optimized for both voice and general-purpose audio, defined in RFC 6716. RFC 7845 defines how to carry it in a continuous logical Ogg bitstream (RFC 3533). Ogg gives Opus metadata, fast and accurate seeking, corruption detection, recapture after errors, low overhead, and the ability to multiplex with other codecs, including video. It also gives a live streamable format identical to the on-disk format.

An Ogg stream is a series of pages, each holding data from one or more packets. A page carries a capture pattern and checksum, start and end flags, and a granule position. One page holds up to 65,025 octets of packet data from up to 255 packets, and packets can be split across pages.

This RFC defines the packet contents, the headers, how packets are organized into a logical stream, and what the granule position means. It does not describe the Ogg container itself.
sections.eli5: Ogg is a shipping crate with numbered shelves. Opus is the music. This paper says exactly how to pack the music so any player can unpack it.

sections.title: How a Stream Is Organized
sections.content:
An Ogg Opus stream has two mandatory header packets. The first packet MUST be the identification (ID) header. It sits alone on the first page, which has the beginning-of-stream flag set. The second packet MUST be the comment header, which holds user-supplied metadata. It MAY span several pages starting on the second page, but it MUST finish the page on which it completes.

Every later page is an audio data page. Each audio data packet contains one Opus packet for each of N streams, where N is typically one for mono or stereo and can be larger for multichannel audio. The first N - 1 Opus packets use the self-delimiting framing from RFC 6716, and the last uses the regular framing. All of them MUST have the same duration.

A logical stream ends with a page whose end-of-stream flag is set, though implementations must cope with truncated streams. No pages may follow an end-of-stream page. If a packet's continuation is broken (for example, page sequence numbers are not consecutive), a demuxer MUST NOT try to decode that packet without special knowledge. A zero-octet audio packet is treated as a malformed Opus packet.
sections.eli5: The first page says what is inside, the second page lists the song details, and every page after that is the music in order. If a piece is missing or torn, the player skips it.

sections.title: Granule Position, Pre-skip and Seeking
sections.content:
The granule position of an audio page counts the PCM samples in the stream up to the last fully decodable sample of the last packet completed on that page. It always counts samples at 48 kHz per channel, because every Opus packet uses a sampling rate that evenly divides 48 kHz. The two header pages have granule position zero, and a page entirely spanned by one packet gets the special value -1. Packet durations are multiples of 2.5 ms up to 120 ms.

Pre-skip is the number of samples a player decodes and then discards at the start, because decoder latency means the first samples are padding rather than real audio. The PCM sample position is the granule position minus pre-skip. For example, a granule position of 59,971 with a pre-skip of 11,971 gives a PCM sample position of 48,000. Dividing by 48000.0 gives the playback time.

The last page can have a granule position that trims audio after the final packet (end trimming). The first audio page may have a granule position larger than its sample count, which allows cropping or joining a live stream, but never smaller unless it is also the end-of-stream page.

To seek, a player does a bisection search on granule positions, then starts decoding at least 3840 samples (80 ms) before the target so the decoder has converged. This pre-roll is separate from pre-skip.

For real-time streams with lost packets, a muxer SHOULD emit packets asking for packet loss concealment, but only gaps that are multiples of 2.5 ms are repairable.
sections.eli5: Every page has a counter that says how much sound came before it, so a player can jump close to any spot. The first moments are throwaway warm-up sound that the player skips.

sections.title: The Identification Header
sections.content:
The ID header starts with the 8-octet magic signature OpusHead. Its fields are:

  • Version (8 bits): MUST be 1 for this specification. The upper four bits are the major version, and implementations SHOULD accept versions 15 or less.
  • Channel Count (8 bits): the number of output channels, never zero.
  • Pre-skip (16 bits, little endian): samples at 48 kHz to discard. At least 3,840 samples (80 ms) is RECOMMENDED when cropping existing streams.
  • Input Sample Rate (32 bits, little endian): the rate of the original input in Hz. It is metadata, not the playback rate, and zero means unspecified.
  • Output Gain (16 bits, signed, little endian): a Q7.8 value in dB that players SHOULD apply by default.
  • Mapping Family (8 bits), followed by an optional channel mapping table.

The mapping table MUST be omitted for family 0 and is required otherwise. An ID header that is too short SHOULD be treated as invalid.
sections.eli5: The first page is the label on the box. It says this is Opus, how many speakers to use, how long the warm-up is, and whether to turn the volume up or down.

sections.title: Channel Mapping
sections.content:
Channel mapping connects the Opus streams inside each packet to the output channels. The table has a Stream Count N (never zero), a Coupled Count M (how many streams decode as stereo) and one octet per output channel that picks which decoded channel to use. The special index 255 means pure silence. For family 0 the table is not coded.

  • Family 0: 1 or 2 channels, mono or stereo, one Opus stream.
  • Family 1: 1 to 8 channels in Vorbis channel order, from mono up to 7.1 surround.
  • Family 255: 1 to 255 channels with no defined meaning; general-purpose players SHOULD NOT play them.
  • Families 2 to 254 are reserved.

A player MUST support any valid mapping of family 0 or 1 even when the channel count does not match its hardware, and SHOULD mix channels up or down as needed. The RFC gives optional stereo downmix matrices for family 1.
sections.eli5: A big song may have many sound tracks, but your speakers might be only two. The mapping is a seating chart that says which sound goes to which speaker, and some seats can stay quiet.

sections.title: The Comment Header and Gain Tags
sections.content:
The comment header starts with the magic signature OpusTags, then follows the Ogg Vorbis comment layout without its final framing bit: a vendor string length and vendor string, a user comment list length, and each comment with its own length. Strings are UTF-8 and lengths are 32-bit little endian. Comments use NAME=value form, such as ARTIST or TITLE.

Two tags are new: R128_TRACK_GAIN and R128_ALBUM_GAIN. Both are Q7.8 values in dB, as an integer from -32768 to 32767 written in ASCII, and each may appear at most once. A player that uses them MUST apply them in addition to the header's output gain. The RFC prefers EBU R128 normalization over older ReplayGain tags, which an Opus comment header SHOULD NOT contain.

An implementation MAY treat a comment header larger than 125,829,120 octets (120 MB) as invalid.
sections.eli5: The second page is the song's name tag: title, artist and so on. Two special tags tell the player how much to turn the volume up or down so all songs sound equally loud.

sections.title: Security and Size Limits
sections.content:
Malicious input can attack codec implementations, so implementations MUST NOT overrun memory or use excessive resources. Header parsing is the most likely place for overruns. A tiny comment header can claim huge string lengths or a huge comment count, so implementations should check available data before allocating memory.

Demuxers SHOULD treat an audio packet larger than 61,440 octets per Opus stream as invalid, unless they have a specific reason to allow extra padding. The RFC derives this limit by taking 8 streams, one stereo stream for each of 8 channels, giving 61,310 octets, and rounding up to a multiple of 1,024.

Seeking to the end to find the duration can become quadratic in the amount of invalid data if rescanning is not careful. Ogg Opus streams SHOULD NOT be used with insecure ciphers or modes vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks, since the capture pattern and magic signatures are predictable.
sections.eli5: A sneaky file might say it holds a mountain of data when it is tiny. Players should check the real size first so they do not try to carry a mountain that is not there.

sections.title: Media Types and IANA Registry
sections.content:
An Ogg Opus file consists of one or more sequentially multiplexed segments, each with exactly one Opus stream. The RECOMMENDED media type is audio/ogg, optionally with codecs=opus, and the RECOMMENDED filename extension is .opus. When Opus is multiplexed with other streams, such as video, .opus is NOT RECOMMENDED. The RFC updates RFC 5334 to add opus as a codecs parameter value.

IANA added .opus as an extension for audio/ogg and created an "Opus Channel Mapping Families" registry under the Specification Required policy. The initial entries are 0, 1 and 255.
sections.eli5: Opus files get the nickname .opus so computers know what they are, and a public list keeps track of the different speaker layouts.

fields.name: Channel Count
fields.desc: Number of output channels; never zero.

fields.name: Pre-skip
fields.desc: Samples at 48 kHz to discard at the start.

fields.name: Input Sample Rate
fields.desc: Original input rate in Hz; zero means unspecified.

fields.name: Output Gain
fields.desc: Q7.8 gain in dB to apply when decoding.

fields.name: Mapping Family
fields.desc: Channel order and meaning; a mapping table follows unless it is 0.

viz.caption: CHANNEL MAPPING FAMILIES DEFINED IN RFC 7845

items.title: Family 0
items.text: 1 or 2 channels, mono or stereo. No mapping table.

items.title: Family 1
items.text: 1 to 8 channels in Vorbis order, up to 7.1 surround.

items.title: Family 255
items.text: 1 to 255 channels with no defined meaning.
